u1-01.title: One stone in the middle
u1-01.prompt: How many liberties does the marked black stone have?
u1-01.hint: Count only the empty points touching the stone along a board line.
u1-01.explanation: The four neighbouring intersections—up, down, left and right—are empty, so this stone has four liberties.

u1-02.title: One stone on the edge
u1-02.prompt: How many liberties does the marked black stone have?
u1-02.hint: The area outside the board cannot be counted.
u1-02.explanation: The black stone has three adjacent empty intersections: left, right and below.

u1-03.title: One stone in the corner
u1-03.prompt: How many liberties does the marked black stone have?
u1-03.hint: A corner has only two board lines leading inward.
u1-03.explanation: Only the points to the right and below are liberties, so the stone has two.

u1-04.title: Two connected stones
u1-04.prompt: How many liberties does this connected black group have?
u1-04.hint: The intersection between the stones is occupied, so it is not a liberty.
u1-04.explanation: Both stones form one group. Count the six different empty intersections around that group.

u1-05.title: Does a diagonal count?
u1-05.prompt: Do the two marked black stones already form one connected group?
u1-05.hint: Stones connect along horizontal or vertical board lines, not across a diagonal.
u1-05.explanation: The stones touch only diagonally. They are still two separate groups.

u1-06.title: Capture in the middle
u1-06.prompt: Black to play. Capture the marked white stone by taking its last liberty.
u1-06.hint: Look for the empty point directly next to White that is not occupied by Black.
u1-06.explanation: Black fills White's final liberty. With no liberties left, the white stone is captured.

u1-07.title: Capture at the edge
u1-07.prompt: Black to play. Find White's last liberty and capture the stone.
u1-07.hint: The board edge gives White no extra liberty. Check the point below it.
u1-07.explanation: The last liberty of this edge stone is directly below it; Black captures there.

u1-08.title: Capture in the corner
u1-08.prompt: Black to play. Capture the white stone in the corner.
u1-08.hint: A corner stone can only gain liberties at the two neighbouring intersections on the board.
u1-08.explanation: The point to the right is occupied by Black. The remaining liberty is below White.

u1-09.title: Capture two stones together
u1-09.prompt: Black to play. Capture the marked pair of connected white stones in one move.
u1-09.hint: Count the empty points around both white stones as one group.
u1-09.explanation: The two white stones share their liberties. Filling the last empty point below the left-hand stone captures the whole group.

u1-10.title: Save a stone in atari
u1-10.prompt: Black to play. Extend the marked black stone to escape atari.
u1-10.hint: The black stone has one liberty left. Check how many liberties the group would have after extending.
u1-10.explanation: Extending downward connects two black stones into one group with more liberties.

u2-01.title: Side-by-side stones
u2-01.prompt: Are the two marked black stones in the same connected group?
u2-01.hint: Follow the horizontal board line between them.
u2-01.explanation: The black stones touch directly along a horizontal line, so they belong to one group.

u2-02.title: Stones above and below
u2-02.prompt: Are the two marked white stones in the same connected group?
u2-02.hint: Follow the vertical board line between them.
u2-02.explanation: The white stones touch directly along a vertical line, so they form one group.

u2-03.title: Diagonal stones remain separate
u2-03.prompt: Are the two marked black stones already one connected group?
u2-03.hint: A diagonal contact is not a direct connection along a board line.
u2-03.explanation: Although they look close, the two stones are still separate groups.

u2-04.title: An opposing stone between them
u2-04.prompt: Are the two marked black stones part of one connected group?
u2-04.hint: Check what occupies the intersection between the black stones.
u2-04.explanation: A white stone separates them. The marked black stones are not directly connected.

u2-05.title: Join across the middle
u2-05.prompt: Black to play. Connect the two marked black stones directly with one move.
u2-05.hint: Find the empty intersection that touches both black stones along the board lines.
u2-05.explanation: Black plays on the shared adjacent point, linking the two stones into one group.

u2-06.title: Join vertically
u2-06.prompt: Black to play. Connect the upper and lower black stones into one group.
u2-06.hint: Check the empty intersection between the two black stones.
u2-06.explanation: Black fills the middle point, making a vertical connection between the stones.

u2-07.title: Connect near the edge
u2-07.prompt: Black to play. Join the two black stones near the left edge.
u2-07.hint: Look for the empty point touching both black stones.
u2-07.explanation: Filling the shared point joins the two stones along the same row.

u2-08.title: A cutting point in the middle
u2-08.prompt: Black to play. Occupy the point where the two marked white stones could connect directly.
u2-08.hint: Find the empty point directly between the two white stones.
u2-08.explanation: Black occupies the middle point, preventing White from connecting there in one move.

u2-09.title: Stop a vertical connection
u2-09.prompt: Black to play. Prevent the upper and lower white stones from connecting directly through the middle.
u2-09.hint: Look for the empty intersection shared by both white stones.
u2-09.explanation: Black occupies that intersection, stopping this direct vertical connection.

u2-10.title: Find the connecting point near the edge
u2-10.prompt: Black to play. Which point would White need to connect the two marked stones directly? Occupy it.
u2-10.hint: Look along the straight line between the two white stones.
u2-10.explanation: Black occupies the point between them, so White cannot connect there in one move.

u4-m01.title: Find the first vital point
u4-m01.prompt: Black to play. Find the point that turns this three-point eye space into two separate real eyes.
u4-m01.hint: Compare the middle point with the two ends. Which move separates the remaining empty space?
u4-m01.explanation: Black plays in the middle, leaving one enclosed empty point on each side. This is the basic straight-three eye-space shape.

u4-m02.title: Rotate the same eye shape
u4-m02.prompt: Black to play. Where is the vital point when the three-point shape is vertical?
u4-m02.hint: Rotating the shape does not change which point divides it into two.
u4-m02.explanation: Black occupies the middle. The top and bottom empty points become separate real eyes.

u4-m03.title: Deny White two eyes
u4-m03.prompt: Black to play. White wants to make two eyes from this connected three-point space. Which vital point should Black take first?
u4-m03.hint: Think about what would happen if White occupied the central point first.
u4-m03.explanation: Black takes the centre so White cannot use that point to split its eye space. White's strongest follow-up still needs to be read.

u4-m04.title: Attack the rotated eye shape
u4-m04.prompt: Black to play. Find the point that prevents White from making two eyes in the vertical shape.
u4-m04.hint: Find the middle of the three connected empty intersections.
u4-m04.explanation: Taking the middle denies White this two-eye formation. The task checks the first vital point, not every later killing variation.

u4-m05.title: Complete a second eye horizontally
u4-m05.prompt: Black to play. The left eye is already enclosed. Fill the missing boundary point of the second eye.
u4-m05.hint: Inspect the four neighbouring points around the right-hand empty eye space.
u4-m05.explanation: Black closes the missing boundary. Both separate empty points become enclosed real eyes.

u4-m06.title: Complete a second eye vertically
u4-m06.prompt: Black to play. Close the missing boundary point of the second eye in this rotated shape.
u4-m06.hint: Confirm the existing eye, then inspect which side of the other eye remains open.
u4-m06.explanation: Filling the gap leaves two separate enclosed eye points. The orientation does not change the condition.

u4-m07.title: Block White's second eye
u4-m07.prompt: Black to play. White is one move away from making a second eye. Occupy the missing boundary point first.
u4-m07.hint: Do not fill the already complete eye. Find the gap around the other candidate eye.
u4-m07.explanation: Black enters the outer gap, so the second empty point touches an opposing stone and is no longer a real white eye.

u4-m08.title: Block the rotated second eye
u4-m08.prompt: Black to play. Occupy the gap in White's second-eye boundary before White can close it.
u4-m08.hint: Compare both candidate eye points. One still has an unclosed boundary.
u4-m08.explanation: Black takes the gap, leaving White with only its existing eye in this task. This alone does not prove the entire group will die.

u3-01.title: A move with no liberties
u3-01.prompt: Black plays a stone that would have no liberties after the move, and no white stones are captured. Is that legal?
options: Yes, any point can be played first
No, it is an illegal self-capture
Yes, but it is risky
u3-01.hint: Imagine the liberties of Black's group after the move.
u3-01.explanation: A move that leaves your group with no liberties and captures nothing is illegal under these rules.

u3-02.title: Capturing removes the problem
u3-02.prompt: Black plays into a surrounded point but captures neighbouring white stones. How should the move be judged?
options: Legal if Black has liberties after the capture
Illegal because the point appeared surrounded
Black must pass instead
u3-02.hint: When you play, remove captured stones before counting your group's remaining liberties.
u3-02.explanation: The captured white stones are removed first. If Black then has liberties, this move is legal.

u3-03.title: Why does ko exist?
u3-03.prompt: Why does the simple ko rule prevent immediate recapture?
options: To prevent a repeating position from continuing forever
To make the board smaller
To ensure Black wins
u3-03.hint: What would happen if each player captured back on every turn?
u3-03.explanation: The ko rule prevents two players from repeating the same board position indefinitely.

u3-04.title: After a ko capture
u3-04.prompt: White has just captured a black stone in a simple ko. What may Black do next?
options: Recapture immediately on that point
Play elsewhere first
Remove White's stone by hand
u3-04.hint: Simple ko forbids the immediate move that recreates the previous position.
u3-04.explanation: Black cannot recapture immediately. Black must play elsewhere first.

u3-05.title: What is a ko threat?
u3-05.prompt: Black plays elsewhere and creates a threat White may have to answer before Black fights for the ko again. What is that move called?
options: A ko threat
An illegal move
An endgame move
u3-05.hint: This threat creates a reason for the opponent to respond before the ko fight continues.
u3-05.explanation: A move that pressures the opponent to answer while fighting a ko is called a ko threat.

u3-06.title: Which ko rule does this app use?
u3-06.prompt: Which repetition restriction does the current interactive rules engine enforce?
options: Simple ko: no immediate return to the preceding board position
Superko: no repetition of any earlier position
No ko restriction
u3-06.hint: The lessons use the common beginner version that looks one board position back.
u3-06.explanation: This engine implements simple ko and prevents an immediate return to the previous board position.

u4-01.title: Why two real eyes matter
u4-01.prompt: A surrounded black group has two separate real eyes that White cannot safely fill. What does this usually tell you?
options: Black is alive in this basic position
Black must be captured
Eyes have no connection to life and death
u4-01.hint: Think about whether White can occupy both eye points without being captured.
u4-01.explanation: Two separate real eyes prevent White from safely filling both spaces in this basic position.

u4-02.title: One eye is not enough
u4-02.prompt: A surrounded group has only one eye. Which conclusion is safest?
options: The group must be alive
The next player and vital points still matter
The group must be dead
u4-02.hint: One eye alone does not guarantee life.
u4-02.explanation: With only one eye, the outcome may depend on who plays first and which vital point they choose.

u4-03.title: A vital point for both sides
u4-03.prompt: A point that stops your opponent from forming a second eye can also help you make one. Which principle is this closest to?
options: Your opponent's vital point may also be yours
The corner is always the smallest area
Capturing always comes first
u4-03.hint: Both players may be fighting for the same eye-shaping point.
u4-03.explanation: In life-and-death positions, both sides may need the same vital point for different reasons.

u4-04.title: A false eye
u4-04.prompt: An empty point looks like an eye, but the opponent can play there safely. How should you treat it?
options: A secure real eye
A false or incomplete eye
An extra liberty that guarantees life
u4-04.hint: A real eye is a space the opponent cannot safely occupy.
u4-04.explanation: A space the opponent can enter safely is not a secure real eye; examine the surrounding stones.

u4-05.title: How to start reading life and death
u4-05.prompt: What is a useful first step when solving a basic life-and-death problem?
options: Find a point that can change the eye shape
Choose any empty point
Count the entire board first
u4-05.hint: Look for a move that could change the local position significantly.
u4-05.explanation: Find a vital point, then consider the opponent's strongest reply rather than stopping at your first idea.

u4-06.title: Who plays first?
u4-06.prompt: In one local position, Black can live when Black plays first, but White can kill when White plays first. What does that show?
options: The order of play can decide life and death
Stone colour makes no difference to the task
One eye is always enough
u4-06.hint: Which player can claim the vital point first?
u4-06.explanation: When an eye shape is unfinished, the player to move can determine whether a group lives.

u5-01.title: Why practice on a 9×9 board?
u5-01.prompt: What is the main benefit of finishing a game on a 9×9 board as a beginner?
options: You can experience the opening, fighting and ending sooner
Half the Go rules disappear
You never need to count liberties
u5-01.hint: A smaller board reaches local fights and the end of the game sooner.
u5-01.explanation: A 9×9 board keeps the rules of Go while making it easier to finish and review a whole game.

u5-02.title: The first goal of the opening
u5-02.prompt: At the beginning of a 9×9 game, which aim is generally more useful?
options: Develop stones with room to grow
Fill the first line immediately
Chase one distant stone at all costs
u5-02.hint: Give your stones room for later moves.
u5-02.explanation: Early moves should build useful space and relationships between stones, rather than start an unnecessary chase.

u5-03.title: What should you notice in the middle game?
u5-03.prompt: One of your groups is surrounded while a small empty corner remains. What should you check first?
options: Whether your surrounded group is in urgent danger
The small empty corner
Whichever area you notice first
u5-03.hint: If a group is lost, the nearby territory may be lost as well.
u5-03.explanation: Check the safety of an urgently weak group before pursuing a smaller gain elsewhere.

u5-04.title: Recognising the endgame
u5-04.prompt: Both players' large groups are mostly safe. Most remaining moves settle a boundary or gain a few points. Which stage does this resemble?
options: The endgame
The opening
The start of a ko fight
u5-04.hint: Notice when the focus shifts from group survival to boundaries.
u5-04.explanation: Settling borders and comparing small territorial gains are typical endgame tasks.

u5-05.title: When both players are ready to stop
u5-05.prompt: Both players believe there are no useful moves left. What is the normal next step?
options: Pass in turn according to the rules and proceed to scoring
Clear the board immediately
Play another move in an empty corner
u5-05.hint: Think about the procedure for ending a game.
u5-05.explanation: After two consecutive passes, the game proceeds to the applicable end-of-game and scoring procedure.

u5-06.title: One useful question after a short game
u5-06.prompt: After a 9×9 game, which review question is most useful for your next game?
options: Which move made my group vulnerable, and what did I overlook?
How many minutes did the game take?
How heavy was my opponent's stone?
u5-06.hint: Look for one decision you can recognise and check next time.
u5-06.explanation: Reviewing one overlooked threat or weak group gives you a concrete question to test in another game.

u6-01.title: Why corners often come first
u6-01.prompt: Why do players often look toward the corners early on an empty board?
options: Two board edges help surround territory more efficiently
A stone in the corner can never be captured
Corner stones have no liberties
u6-01.hint: In a corner, you have fewer sides to enclose than in the centre.
u6-01.explanation: The two board edges make it possible to secure an area with fewer stones. This is a useful opening principle, not an absolute rule.

u6-02.title: Develop toward friendly support
u6-02.prompt: You already have a stone in one corner. Why might you extend toward nearby friendly stones?
options: Your new and existing stones can support one another
Your stones should always be as far apart as possible
The only aim is to add one liberty
u6-02.hint: Notice whether the new stone gives your existing stones a useful direction.
u6-02.explanation: Moves that work with nearby friendly stones tend to develop more effectively than isolated moves.

u6-03.title: No universally best opening point
u6-03.prompt: Someone says the star point is always better than the 3–4 point. What is the best response?
options: Neither is always best; consider the board and your plan
Yes, the same point is best in every game
That rule applies only to 9×9 boards
u6-03.hint: Opening patterns depend on the position, not a single memorised coordinate.
u6-03.explanation: Both the star point and the 3–4 point have legitimate uses. Their value depends on nearby stones and the overall plan.

u6-04.title: Look nearby before extending
u6-04.prompt: Before deciding which side to extend toward, what should you examine?
options: Nearby friendly and opposing stones, and the available space
How shiny the stones are
Which player first picked up a stone
u6-04.hint: Support and pressure from other stones change how an extension works.
u6-04.explanation: Nearby stones show which direction offers room to develop and which direction invites an attack.

u6-05.title: Urgent or simply large?
u6-05.prompt: One of your groups is under pressure, but there is also a large open area elsewhere. What should you compare first?
options: Whether the pressured group needs an urgent move
Which empty area has the nicest colour
Whether the board looks symmetrical
u6-05.hint: A large opening point may be less important than a group in immediate trouble.
u6-05.explanation: Compare the urgency of protecting the weak group with the value of the open area. A truly urgent threat often comes first.

u6-06.title: A question after every opening move
u6-06.prompt: After an opening move, which question is most useful?
options: How does this move work with my nearby stones?
How many centimetres is it from the centre?
Can this move capture something immediately?
u6-06.hint: The value of an opening stone often comes from its relationship to other stones.
u6-06.explanation: Checking how the move supports existing stones gives a more reliable sense of direction than examining the stone alone.

u7-01.title: What counts as territory?
u7-01.prompt: Which description best matches reasonably secure territory?
options: An area with fairly clear boundaries that can be counted
Any single isolated stone
A large central space neither player has settled
u7-01.hint: Look for an area whose ownership is relatively clear.
u7-01.explanation: Secure territory has boundaries firm enough that its points can be counted with reasonable confidence.

u7-02.title: What is thickness?
u7-02.prompt: Which position best illustrates thickness in Go?
options: A safe, solid shape that can support play farther out
A group in atari with only one liberty
An area whose points are already guaranteed
u7-02.hint: Thickness is about safety and what your stones can help you do next.
u7-02.explanation: A thick group is relatively secure and can support fighting or development nearby; it does not have a fixed point value.

u7-03.title: Thickness is not a fixed number
u7-03.prompt: If you build a thick wall, does that automatically mean you are many points ahead?
options: No; its value depends on how it can be used across the board
Yes; each thick stone is worth exactly ten points
Yes, provided the wall is in a corner
u7-03.hint: A wall needs useful targets or room in which to exert influence.
u7-03.explanation: Thickness has no fixed conversion into territory. The nearby weak groups and open space determine how valuable it may become.

u7-04.title: Trading territory for influence
u7-04.prompt: An exchange gives you more immediate territory but gives your opponent outside influence. What should you examine before judging it?
options: Where the influence points and whether it has useful targets
Which player has more individual stones
The colour of the wooden board frame
u7-04.hint: Influence matters most when it can affect actual positions.
u7-04.explanation: Judge both sides of the exchange in context: how secure is the territory, and can the opponent use the outside strength?

u7-05.title: Do not fight a strong wall blindly
u7-05.prompt: Why can fighting right beside an opponent's solid, thick wall be dangerous?
options: Their nearby strength gives them support in the fight
The rules forbid playing next to a wall
The wall automatically removes your liberties
u7-05.hint: Consider which player's stones are better supported.
u7-05.explanation: The opponent's solid wall may make their fighting stones safer and leave you with fewer useful options.

u7-06.title: Compare the whole board
u7-06.prompt: Which is the least reliable way to compare territory with thickness?
options: Assign every thick wall one fixed point value
Look at the surrounding groups
Look for directions in which the position can develop
u7-06.hint: The usefulness of thickness changes with the position.
u7-06.explanation: Thickness cannot be valued by one universal point formula; assess the nearby groups and potential development.
